newsitem.title: MACAU: Stamp-sized Macau is a philately boomtown.
newsitem.headline: Stamp-sized Macau is a philately boomtown.

text.p: On most maps of the world, Macau is smaller than a postage stamp, but the Portuguese-run territory has many bigger places licked when it comes to stamp collecting.
Stamps trigger stampedes, sell like hotcakes and can gain nine times their face value in a day because of the high artistic quality and limited issues.
More than 5,000 people, about one percent of Macau's population, scrambled to join the queue for the latest first-day covers and souvenir sheets on October 21.
Police were called in to keep the crowd in order outside the central post office on the usually sleepy main thoroughfare of Avenida de Almeida Ribeoiro.
"We offer good printing quality, attractive designs and themes and the commemorative issues are strictly limited," Macau postal chief Carlos Alberto Roldao Lopes told Reuters.
Ballooning collector interest in Macau stamps may also have been triggered by the enclave's looming handover to China.

After more than four centuries of Portuguese rule, Macau becomes a Special Administrative Region of China in December 1999, two years after neighbouring British-ruled Hong Kong where stamp fever also runs high.
The latest philatelic issues in Macau consist of five richly coloured stamps featuring traditional Chinese paper kites.
A souvenir sheet of the issue was sold for eight patacas ($1) but is now worth 60 patacas on the stamp market.
Many in the queue were elderly residents and new immigrants. Many had queued overnight. Some held babies in their arms. On many minds was a quick sale to dealers.
The post office limited sales to just a few items per person to prevent professionals from joining the crowd.
"Our themes pay attention to Macau's specific cultural heritage that combines Chinese, Portuguese and local Macanese elements," Lopes said.
"Our issues are limited to between 200,000 to 500,000 to ensure our stamps have a certain rarity value," said Maria de Lourdes Almeida, a colleague of Lopes.
Philatelic sales had become an important additional source of income for the government, she said. Official sources have put the figure at over 20 million patacas for last year.
The postal department has contracted philatelic agents in Germany, Britain, Sweden, Hong Kong, Portugal and elsewhere.

Bona fide collectors and hard-core investors in China and Taiwan have become players in the Macau stamp markets. "We don't know how many of our clients are investors, or just philatelists who like the quality," Lopes said.
The department began launching philatelic issues in earnest in the the early 1980s in order to generate revenue.
Seven commemorative issues were launched in 1990. This year there are a total of 41 stamps. In 1997, 13 issues are planned.

While Macau's first stamp was issued by Lisbon back in 1884, local artists have been hired only since the 1970s. But Macau stamps continue to be printed in Portugal for the sake of quality and security.
Macau stamps do not bear the Portuguese national emblem but merely the words Republica Portuguesa.
"The reference to the Portuguese Republic will have to be deleted after the reversion to Chinese rule," Lopes said.
"Macau stamps are valuable because their issues are limited. That is good for philatelists and investors alike," local philatelist Ho Weng Hong told Reuters.
Ho owns two of Macau's most expensive stamps, each worth about US$10,000, which he keeps in a bank vault.

"The blue stamps were issued for Macau in Lisbon in 1911, a year after Portugal's republican revolution, and because they show the last Portuguese King Dom Carlos they printed a black bar on them," Ho explained.
"I bought the two stamps in the United States eight years ago for just about US$1,500 each from a dealer, and now each is worth about 80,000 patacas," he said.
Only 28 of these stamps are known to exist, seven of them owned by individuals and the remaining 21 kept at the Macau Post Office Museum.
Ho said local stamps could usually be sold to dealers at more than eight times their face value on the day of issue.
"Some dealers wait outside the post office when new stamps are being launched, offering good prices to private buyers."
Some stamps with a face value of 10 patacas to mark the current Chinese Year of the Rat now had a market value of 90 patacas.
